title: torch.compile slower or failing for GNN training with NeighborLoader dynamic batches
body: I am benchmarking a simple GCN trained with PyG NeighborLoader, where every mini-batch has dynamic node and edge counts. Basic gather/scatter compile tests pass with static and dynamic shapes, but in this end-to-end benchmark eager mode is faster than torch.compile, and the logs show repeated TorchDynamo recompilations and cache-size-limit warnings. I am using a PyTorch 1.14 development build with CUDA 12 on A100 GPUs. Is torch.compile expected to handle this dynamic NeighborLoader workload?

symptoms_visible: A simple GCN trained with NeighborLoader takes about 0.84 seconds per epoch in eager mode, while torch.compile is slower and emits cache-size-limit warnings for changing tensor sizes and strides.
N0.label: N0 dynamic NeighborLoader slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: With dynamic=True, compilation fails with SymInt-related exceptions instead of completing training; an early run with the patched training branch on the container also segfaults.
N1.label: N1 dynamic training failure characterized

symptoms_visible: After rebuilding from the proposed training branch with a current Triton source build, dynamic=True still fails; adding the specialize_int_float hack gets farther but backward then crashes with an AttributeError involving symbolic sizes and strides.
N2.label: N2 proposed patches falsified

symptoms_visible: A second GNN training reproduction also fails during compiled backward; after intervening fixes, execution can reach the end only when split reductions are disabled, but compiled execution remains slower than eager and still shows specialization warnings.
N3.label: N3 dynamic-shape failure chain isolated

symptoms_visible: The PyG static benchmark reports a large compiled speedup, but the NeighborLoader reproduction remains slower even with fixed input sizes or jittable layers; under a synchronized standard benchmark runner, dynamic-shape Inductor is only about 1.02x faster.
N4.label: N4 performance measurements reconciled

symptoms_visible: With current PyTorch, PyG, PyG-lib, and Triton builds, the reporter's actual NeighborLoader training script completes under torch.compile and measures about a 20% speedup over eager mode.
N5.label: N5 reporter verifies current NeighborLoader improvement

symptoms_visible: The dynamic NeighborLoader training workload runs successfully on the updated compiler stack and the reporter has verified an approximately 20% speedup using the real training script.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Is this inference only, or does the benchmark include training and backward?
Does the failure occur while training the GNN?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is training. Each epoch includes the forward pass, loss.backward(), and the optimizer step.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It is inference-only with fixed inputs and never calls backward.

question_patterns: What happens when you explicitly compile with dynamic=True?
Does dynamic=True avoid the recompilations or produce a different failure?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With dynamic=True, eager is about 0.72 seconds per epoch, but torch.compile raises SymInt-related errors, including an unhashable SymInt and later Tensor.size receiving a SymInt where it expects an integer dimension.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: dynamic=True completes reliably and is substantially faster than eager.
dynamic=True fails with the same SymInt exception but at a slightly different stack-frame location.

question_patterns: Are you using the old Triton backend or the newer MLIR backend?
Which Triton revision is installed in the container?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The February container was using the older Triton backend pinned near the beginning of the month. I can rebuild the proposed PyTorch branch with the latest Triton source.

edges.comment: The first investigation established that this is compiled training with backward, not inference, and separated the explicit dynamic=True failure from the initial recompilation slowdown.

question_patterns: Can you rebuild with the training fix from PR 93059 and the latest Triton, then rerun the benchmark?
Does the failure remain with the proposed AOTAutograd patch and new Triton backend?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I built the PR branch and installed the latest Triton source build. Without dynamic=True it still recompiles until the cache limit, and with dynamic=True it still fails.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The rebuilt branch with current Triton runs the full dynamic training workload and is faster than eager.

question_patterns: Please apply the specialize_int_float=True eval-frame patch and test it together with PR 93059.
Does the suggested dynamic-shape configuration hack unblock the full forward and backward pass?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. The patch gets past the earlier error, but loss.backward() fails in the compiled backward path with AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute '_has_symbolic_sizes_strides'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The hack and PR complete all epochs and provide a stable speedup.
The eager timing changes by a few milliseconds after rebuilding.

edges.comment: These were handler-requested build and patch measurements. They falsified treating PR 93059 or the specialize_int_float hack as a complete solution.

question_patterns: Can the failing scatter/broadcast path be reduced to a smaller reproduction?
Does another dynamic mini-batch GNN training workload fail in the same compiled backward area?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A second affected GNN user reproduced the compiled-backward failure on PyTorch 2.0 development builds and reduced the relevant PyG scatter path. A repro collected after AOT also showed the related case where one compiled input unexpectedly becomes None.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The reduced scatter path works, and the only failing operation is a custom extension outside PyTorch.

edges.comment: Composite-user simplification: the second affected GNN reporter is folded into the simulated user side. Engineer investigation additionally established that PR 96219 fixed the None-input failure, while dynamic split reductions introduced static guards and overspecialization; disabling split reductions reached completion but was explicitly considered a poor performance workaround.

question_patterns: Can you share the PyG benchmark that reports the large static compilation speedup?
What result are you comparing the NeighborLoader workload against?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The PyG basic-GNN benchmark showed more than 2x speedup for some static cases, and I shared its result and source. It uses jittable convolution instances for static compilation.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same static benchmark shows a smaller but still positive speedup on another A100.

question_patterns: Does converting the GraphConv layers with jittable() reproduce the static benchmark's speedup?
Please try jittable convolution instances in the NeighborLoader script; does that fix its performance?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. Both maintainers confirmed that jittable() does not help this NeighborLoader case; one run became slightly slower.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: jittable() makes the NeighborLoader model consistently more than twice as fast as eager.

question_patterns: What performance do you get when the basic GNN test is run under the standard benchmark runner with forward and backward included?
Can you compare static, CUDAGraph, and dynamic-shape Inductor using consistent timing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On an A100 source build, the basic benchmark showed modest improvements rather than a universal 2x result. The standardized measurements were about 1.267x for static Inductor with CUDAGraphs, 1.102x for static Inductor without CUDAGraphs, and 1.021x for dynamic-shape Inductor.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The synchronized standard runner confirms a repeatable 2x dynamic-shape speedup.

edges.comment: The engineer also noticed that the original NeighborLoader timer omitted CUDA synchronization and that torch_geometric.profile synchronized between forward and backward, explaining much of the discrepancy between apparent benchmark speedups. Static-input and jittable experiments did not solve the reported workload.

question_patterns: Can you rerun the actual NeighborLoader training benchmark with current PyTorch, PyG, PyG-lib, and Triton?
After the recent compiler fixes, does your original dynamic mini-batch workload complete and outperform eager?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I tested the current stack with the same NeighborLoader GCN training script and now get about a 20% speedup using the OpenAI Triton backend.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The current stack still crashes in backward or remains slower than eager on the original NeighborLoader script.
The current stack completes with an 18% rather than 20% speedup.

edges.comment: This is the decisive reporter-side verification on the real dynamic NeighborLoader workload, rather than a static microbenchmark.

solution.intent: Resolve the issue on the updated PyTorch/PyG/Triton stack, where cumulative dynamic-shape and compiled-backward fixes allow the real NeighborLoader training workload to run, and evaluate performance with synchronized end-to-end measurements rather than the misleading static benchmark comparison.
solution.concrete_example: Use current PyTorch, PyG, PyG-lib, and Triton builds, compile the GCN with dynamic-shape support, and benchmark the complete NeighborLoader forward/backward/optimizer workload with correct CUDA synchronization. The reporter's script now completes and shows roughly a 20% speedup; retain a NeighborLoader case in the standard benchmark suite to track dynamic-shape overhead.

edges.comment: Resolution is grounded in cumulative compiler fixes and the reporter's May verification. The result is a measured improvement of about 20%, not the earlier hoped-for universal 2x speedup.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause as a combination of immature dynamic-shape and compiled-backward handling for variable NeighborLoader batches— including symbolic-size failures, insufficient or overspecialized guards around reductions, recompilation/graph-break overhead—and not as a generic inability of GNN operations to compile.

Must ground the conclusion in the collected evidence: dynamic=True SymInt failures, failure of PR 93059 plus the specialize_int_float hack, the second user's backward reproduction, the split-reduction/guard investigation, and the reporter's successful current-stack rerun.

Must explain that the apparent large static speedup was not directly applicable to NeighborLoader and was partly distorted by CUDA synchronization methodology; performance must be measured on the full synchronized forward/backward/optimizer workload.
Must not present PR 93059, specialize_int_float=True, disabling split reductions, or GraphConv.jittable() as the final fix: each was insufficient or explicitly undesirable in this case.
Must recommend the current PyTorch, PyG, PyG-lib, and Triton stack and acknowledge the verified result as approximately a 20% NeighborLoader speedup rather than promising a universal 2x gain.
Must treat the issue as resolved only after the reporter verifies that the original dynamic NeighborLoader training script completes and outperforms eager.

persona_hint.experience_level: ML framework and container benchmark developer familiar with building PyTorch and Triton from source, changing compiler configuration, running development branches, and comparing GNN training performance, but relies on compiler maintainers for Dynamo and Inductor internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, practical, and cooperative; supplies full traces and benchmark links, tests requested patches and source builds, corrects earlier test assumptions, and asks for realistic performance timelines.
